clinicalPearls: A common cause of heel pain in physically active children and early adolescents, related to traction at the calcaneal growth plate
Pain is felt at the back and sides of the heel, worse with running and jumping and eased by rest
It typically occurs during the growth spurt and often around a period of increased sporting activity
The squeeze test, compressing the sides of the calcaneus, reproduces the pain
It is a self-limiting condition that resolves once the calcaneal apophysis fuses
Management is with activity modification, calf stretching, heel cushioning and reassurance
reference.pathophysiology: Sever's disease is a traction apophysitis of the calcaneus, in which repetitive tensile load from the Achilles tendon on the still-open calcaneal growth plate, combined with the impact of running and jumping, produces stress and inflammation at the apophysis. The vulnerability of the growth plate during the adolescent growth spurt, when bone growth may outpace muscle-tendon flexibility, increases traction across the apophysis. It is a benign, self-limiting overuse condition rather than a structural or destructive process.
additionalDifferentials: Bone cyst or tumour of the calcaneus
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the age, activity and positive squeeze test
Radiographs only to exclude other pathology if the picture is atypical
Assessment of calf flexibility and footwear
Further imaging if there are red flags for another diagnosis
redFlags: Night pain, rest pain or systemic features suggesting infection or tumour
Failure to settle with appropriate measures
Significant unilateral symptoms without a clear activity link
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and resolves spontaneously with skeletal maturity, and symptoms are well controlled in the meantime with conservative measures.
pitfalls: Missing a calcaneal stress fracture, infection or tumour when features are atypical
Failing to address calf tightness and training load
Advising complete rest rather than activity modification
management: Reassure the child and family that it is benign and resolves with skeletal maturity once the apophysis fuses
Relative rest and reduction of training load during painful periods
Heel cushions, heel raises, or shock-absorbing insoles to offload the apophysis
Simple analgesia such as paracetamol or NSAIDs for symptom control during flares
Footwear review and graded return to sport as pain settles
Reserve radiographs or further imaging for atypical or persistent presentations to exclude other pathology
